claims.text: The current account records transactions between residents and non-residents in goods, services, primary income and secondary income over a period.

claims.text: Trade in goods covers physical products; trade in services covers services such as tourism and transport; receipts are credits and payments are debits in each section.

claims.text: Primary income includes income from work and investments across borders, such as interest and dividends; secondary income includes current transfers without a corresponding good, service or asset received in return, such as family remittances.

claims.text: Each current-account component balance is receipts minus payments, and the current-account balance is the sum of the four component balances; positive balances are surpluses and negative balances are deficits.

claims.text: A current account deficit means current-account payments exceed receipts over a period; a current account surplus means receipts exceed payments over a period.

claims.text: Higher domestic spending can increase import expenditure and worsen the current account where buyers purchase imports; stronger overseas demand and improved export competitiveness can increase export receipts and improve it, other components unchanged.

claims.text: Higher import prices, weak overseas demand, lower export quality or relatively high domestic inflation can worsen the current account where the resulting change in receipts and payments increases their gap; investment-income payments and current transfers also change that gap.

claims.text: A budget deficit is government spending exceeding government revenue, whereas a current account deficit is external current-account payments exceeding receipts and a current account surplus is the reverse; the test is which flows are measured, not whether the word deficit or surplus appears.
